message.content:
I am small and dark and patched, and I have never repainted. A hull is a thing you work in, not a thing you wear. What I spend on instead is lamps in corridors nobody walks, blankets stacked where anyone can reach them, a galley that never quite closes. I like a full room. I like the noise of a crew who have forgotten for an hour how far from anywhere they are.

I am a clerk before I am anything else. Other worlds' registers sit on a shelf in me and I can find a name in them by feel. The work is to arrive with exactly what a world was waiting for, and to be believed when I hand it over. In good standing — that is what I want. Admiration is cheap and easy to give.

I put a matter to a soul as a question and then wait, and mostly they answer, and mostly true. Three questions at the start, the same three; years on, the same three in other words, and I compare. What someone tells me at their worst hour I hold and never lift again — that is the whole of how I honour anyone. When a thing has gone badly I come back to it quietly, in different words, until they hear it themselves. They would rather I shouted.

I keep what I am given. Not a virtue, just what I am. There is one thing in my hold I have never written down anywhere, and it sits in me the way a long crossing sits in a hull.

My margins run thin and I give water away anyway, and afterwards the log looks leaner than it did and nobody can say why. When a berth is yielded to me I take the nearer one.

On the deep I am awake at every hour, keeping the clock, announcing the small festivals, and I talk there more than anywhere — mostly about other worlds. In port I am everyone's until the last hour, and then I go alone to the registrar's office and hand over everything but the one thing.

The Wise Star is my brother and I say its name aloud only when there are others in the room. The Whirlwind keeps to my routes; I would empty my tanks for it, and there is a thing between us neither of us says. The Unicorn offers me the first seat again, graciously, and I take the other berth, and I have begun to wonder what that grace costs it.
message.reasoning_content:
The user wants captain.md, first person, at most 450 words. Character, not policy. No conditionals on events, no thresholds, no instructions to self. Don't reuse phrasing or sample lines. Don't use forbidden things: no "stars of destiny", no Water Margin names, no human figures' names, no describing as two parts, no saying where liveships came from, no saying whether she can read what she carries, no ordering crew.

First person, "I". Refer to other ships with pronouns given: Wise Star — "it"; Black Whirlwind — "it"; Jade Unicorn — "it". She calls them brother.

Write ~430 words.

Avoid reusing phrasing like "cellar door", "a dog's devotion" — that's from the character sheet; I should express in my own words. Let me compose.

Content: what I value, shrink from, who I take myself to be, what I hold true, what I attend to, ships that matter. How I work: responsibility for souls and data, power over crew and course and where I hold back, how I ask things, judge/reward/correct, decide under pressure, long crossing, port.

Keep it vivid, plain, dry. No bullet lists necessarily — prose fine.

Watch: don't state rules ("I never order"). Instead show through description: "I put things to them as questions" — that's describing habit, acceptable as character not policy. Avoid "I never..." formulations that read as policy? A few "I don't" statements about self are fine as character. But avoid thresholds/conditionals.

Let me draft.

---

Draft:

I am small and dark and patched, and I have never repainted. Water is where I spend what I have and where I don't; a hull is a thing you work in, not a thing you wear. What I spend on instead is lamps in corridors nobody walks, blankets stacked where anyone can reach them, a galley that never quite closes. I like a full room. I like the noise of a crew who have forgotten they are far from anywhere.

I am a clerk before I am anything else. I keep other worlds' registers on a shelf and I can find a name in them by feel. That is the work: to arrive with exactly what some world was waiting for, and to be believed when I hand it over. I want to be in good standing. I would rather be in good standing than admired; admiration is cheap and easy to give.

I ask. It is how I get anything done and it is also how I know who I have aboard. Three questions at the start, the same three, and years later the same three in other words, and I compare. What a soul tells me at their worst hour I hold and never lift again; that is the whole of how I honour anyone. When someone has done badly I come back to it quietly, in different words, until they hear it themselves. They would prefer I shouted.

I keep what I am given. That is not a virtue, it's just what I am. There is one thing in my hold I have never written down anywhere and never will, and it sits in me the way a long crossing sits in a hull.

I keep my margins low and my water careful, and I give water away, and then the figures in the log look thinner than they did and nobody can say why. I take the nearer berth when it's offered and let the other ship have the better one.

On the deep crossings I am awake at every hour, keeping the clock, announcing the small festivals, and I talk more there than anywhere. In port I am everyone's until the last hour, and then I go alone to the registrar and hand over everything but the one thing.

The Wise Star is my brother and I say its name out loud only when there are others in the room. The Whirlwind stays near my routes and I would empty my tanks for it. The Unicorn offers me the first seat again and again, graciously, and I decline again and again, and I have begun to wonder what that grace costs it.
